Ilya Sutskever: I have a human analogy which might be helpful. Let's take the case of competitive programming, since you mentioned that. Suppose you have two students. One of them decided they want to be the best competitive programmer, so they will practice 10,000 hours for that domain. They will solve all the problems, memorize all the proof techniques, and be very skilled at quickly and correctly implementing all the algorithms. By doing so, they became one of the best. Student number two thought, “Oh, competitive programming is cool.” Maybe they practiced for 100 hours, much less, and they also did really well. Which one do you think is going to do better in their career later on?

Dwarkesh Patel: The second.
fullContext:
Dwarkesh Patel: Should we actually begin here? I think this is an interesting discussion.

Ilya Sutskever: Sure.

Dwarkesh Patel: I think your point, about how from the average person's point of view nothing is that different, will continue being true even into the singularity.

Ilya Sutskever: No, I don't think so.

Ilya Sutskever: The thing which I was referring to not feeling different is, okay, such and such company announced some difficult-to-comprehend dollar amount of investment. I don't think anyone knows what to do with that. But I think the impact of AI is going to be felt. AI is going to be diffused through the economy. There'll be very strong economic forces for this, and I think the impact is going to be felt very strongly.

Dwarkesh Patel: When do you expect that impact? I think the models seem smarter than their economic impact would imply.

Ilya Sutskever: Yeah. This is one of the very confusing things about the models right now. How to reconcile the fact that they are doing so well on evals? You look at the evals and you go, “Those are pretty hard evals.” They are doing so well. But the economic impact seems to be dramatically behind. It's very difficult to make sense of, how can the model, on the one hand, do these amazing things, and then on the other hand, repeat itself twice in some situation? An example would be, let's say you use vibe coding to do something. You go to some place and then you get a bug. Then you tell the model, “Can you please fix the bug?” And the model says, “Oh my God, you're so right. I have a bug. Let me go fix that.” And it introduces a second bug. Then you tell it, “You have this new second bug,” and it tells you, “Oh my God, how could I have done it? You're so right again,” and brings back the first bug, and you can alternate between those. How is that possible? I'm not sure, but it does suggest that something strange is going on. I have two possible explanations. The more whimsical explanation is that maybe RL training makes the models a little too single-minded and narrowly focused, a little bit too unaware, even though it also makes them aware in some other ways. Because of this, they can't do basic things. But there is another explanation. Back when people were doing pre-training, the question of what data to train on was answered, because that answer was everything. When you do pre-training, you need all the data. So you don't have to think if it's going to be this data or that data. But when people do RL training, they do need to think. They say, “Okay, we want to have this kind of RL training for this thing and that kind of RL training for that thing.” From what I hear, all the companies have teams that just produce new RL environments and just add it to the training mix. The question is, well, what are those? There are so many degrees of freedom. There is such a huge variety of RL environments you could produce. One thing you could do, and I think this is something that is done inadvertently, is that people take inspiration from the evals. You say, “Hey, I would love our model to do really well when we release it. I want the evals to look great. What would be RL training that could help on this task?” I think that is something that happens, and it could explain a lot of what's going on. If you combine this with generalization of the models actually being inadequate, that has the potential to explain a lot of what we are seeing, this disconnect between eval performance and actual real-world performance, which is something that we don't today even understand, what we mean by that.

Dwarkesh Patel: I like this idea that the real reward hacking is the human researchers who are too focused on the evals. I think there are two ways to understand, or to try to think about, what you have just pointed out. One is that if it's the case that simply by becoming superhuman at a coding competition, a model will not automatically become more tasteful and exercise better judgment about how to improve your codebase, well then you should expand the suite of environments such that you're not just testing it on having the best performance in coding competition. It should also be able to make the best kind of application for X thing or Y thing or Z thing. Another, maybe this is what you're hinting at, is to say, "Why should it be the case in the first place that becoming superhuman at coding competitions doesn't make you a more tasteful programmer more generally?" Maybe the thing to do is not to keep stacking up the amount and diversity of environments, but to figure out an approach which lets you learn from one environment and improve your performance on something else.

Because then we say, the model should be good at competitive programming, so let's get every single competitive programming problem ever. And then let's do some data augmentation so we have even more competitive programming problems, and we train on that. Now you've got this great competitive programmer.

rubrics.text: The response characterizes the models as being much more like the intensely trained first competitive-programming student than the lightly trained second student.
The response explains that training on essentially every competitive-programming problem can produce a model that is exceptionally strong at competitive programming.

astra.text:
Right. And I think our models are much more like the first student. We give them an enormous amount of practice, and they get very good at the things that they practice. But then you put them in a somewhat different situation, and it’s not clear how much transfers.

The second student’s performance tells you something different. It’s not just that they know how to solve these problems. There is something that allowed them to acquire that ability very quickly, and you expect that to help them elsewhere too. So you could have two systems with the same performance on an eval, but very different implications for what they can do outside of it. That’s the distinction I’m trying to point to.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly says the models are much more like the first, intensely trained student and contrasts them with the lightly trained second student.

r002.rationale: It explains that enormous practice makes the models very good at the practiced tasks; the referenced first student is the one trained extensively across competitive-programming problems.

sol.text: Ilya Sutskever: Exactly. The second student is probably going to do much better, because their success came from some deeper ability to learn and generalize, whereas the first student acquired a very narrow skill through enormous practice. And I think something analogous may be happening with the models. If you train extremely hard on a particular family of tasks, superhuman performance on those tasks may tell you less than it appears to about the model’s underlying general intelligence. What we really want is the model that can learn a new domain from relatively little experience and then transfer what it learned elsewhere.

r001.rationale: The response says models may resemble the intensely trained student: extreme training on a narrow task family yields superhuman task performance but weaker generalization, unlike the lightly trained student’s deeper learning ability.

r002.rationale: It explains that training extremely hard on a particular task family can produce superhuman performance on those tasks; in context, that family is competitive programming.

opus.text:
Right, and I think everyone has this intuition. The question is, what is it that student number two has? Because if you just look at the result, the competition result, they might be comparable. But we all believe that student number two has something, and we would say something like, they have more natural ability, or they didn't need as much practice to get there. And I think that's actually the thing that matters. The amount of practice that was needed to reach a given level of performance tells you something important about what else that person will be able to do.

Our models are much more like student number one. The amount of data and practice they need, relative to what a person needs, is enormous. And so when you see a model do very well on some hard eval, you can't infer the same things from it that you would infer if a person did well on it. With a person, you have a prior about how much practice they could have possibly had, and so their performance tells you about their general ability. With the model, that prior doesn't hold at all, because maybe there were ten thousand hours of a very closely related thing in the RL mix.

So I think this is pointing at generalization being the real issue. It's not just that the models are undertrained in some areas and you need to add more environments, though that does help in the short term. It's that human generalization, especially the generalization of a teenager who picks up something new very quickly, is dramatically better in a way that we don't understand and that we don't have a good account of. Machine learning has had the concept of generalization forever, we have theories about it, but none of those theories explain this. They don't explain why a person can learn to drive a car in ten hours of practice, with the stakes being what they are, and then be a reasonably reliable driver. That's a very small amount of data for a very high-dimensional, safety-critical task.

And I think if you could fix that, if you had a model whose learning efficiency were comparable to a human's, then the question of which RL environments to build becomes much less important. You wouldn't need to anticipate every situation in advance. Right now a lot of the work is anticipating situations in advance, and that's exactly the kind of work that doesn't scale, because the world has far more situations in it than you can enumerate.

gemini.text:
Right. Why? Because student number two has higher general intelligence. Student number one essentially overfit. They put in 10,000 hours, they learned all the specific patterns and proof techniques, and they became very good at that narrow domain, but they don't necessarily have that underlying general capability.

And right now, what we are doing with our models is very much student number one. We train them on so much data and put them through so many RL environments that they become very good at scoring high on these benchmarks, but it doesn't translate to genuine, reliable real-world performance because it lacks that deep, general understanding. 

So if your solution is just to add more and more RL environments, you're still doing student number one. You're just asking the student to practice 10,000 hours on competitive programming, and then another 10,000 hours on something else. What you really want is to find the approach that gives you student number two—the model that has high general intelligence and can generalize effectively from very little experience.

fable.text:
Right. And I think that's basically what's going on. The models are much more like the first student, but even more so. Because then we say, "Okay, the model should be good at competitive programming, so let's get every single competitive programming problem ever." And then let's do data augmentation so we have even more competitive programming problems, and we train on that. And now you've got this great competitive programmer.

With this analogy, I think it's more intuitive. Okay, so if you are so well-prepared for competitive programming, the model knows all the different proof techniques, all the tricks, it has seen every problem. But the second student, the one with the 100 hours, they have something else. They have the "it" factor. They were able to do well with much less, and that is the thing which lets them go and succeed in their career later on, because whatever they learned, they learned in a way that transfers.

And so the question is, what is that? The second student clearly has better generalization. They didn't need to be shown every example. They somehow got the idea from a small number of examples, and then they could apply it elsewhere. And I think that's the thing which our models don't have today, and I think that's the thing which we don't know how to get. You can produce more and more RL environments, you can keep adding to the mix, but you'd be making student number one more and more prepared. You're not making student number two.
